title: Given a binary tree and a target sum, determine whether the tree has any root-to-leaf path such that adding up all the node values along the path equals the target sum. Return true or false, and explain why a depth-first traversal is the natural fit for this problem.
shortTitle: Binary Tree Path Sum (Does a Root-to-Leaf Path Equal a Target?)

s1_definition.profdef: Binary Tree Path Sum is a Tree Depth First Search problem where we walk from the root down to each leaf, subtracting each node's value from the running target as we descend. The answer is true if and only if we reach a leaf node where the remaining target exactly equals that leaf's value. The traversal is recursive and visits every node once, so it runs in linear time in the number of nodes with recursion-stack space proportional to the height of the tree.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine at the National Bank of India there is an approval hierarchy. Rajesh submits a request and it flows down a chain of approvers, and each approver adds a fee. We want to know if there is any complete top-to-bottom chain whose total fee adds up to exactly the budget we set aside. We follow one chain all the way to the bottom, keep subtracting each fee from the budget, and when we reach the final approver we check if the budget landed exactly at zero.
s1_definition.oneliner: Walk each root-to-leaf path depth first, subtract as you go, and declare success when a leaf makes the remainder exactly zero.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Binary Tree Path Sum is a Tree Depth First Search problem where we walk from the root down to each leaf, subtracting each node's value from the running target as we descend. The answer is true if and only if we reach a leaf node where the remaining target exactly equals that leaf's value. The traversal is recursive and visits every node once, so it runs in linear time in the number of nodes with recursion-stack space proportional to the height of the tree.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine at the National Bank of India there is an approval hierarchy. Rajesh submits a request and it flows down a chain of approvers, and each approver adds a fee. We want to know if there is any complete top-to-bottom chain whose total fee adds up to exactly the budget we set aside. We follow one chain all the way to the bottom, keep subtracting each fee from the budget, and when we reach the final approver we check if the budget landed exactly at zero.

**One line to remember:** Walk each root-to-leaf path depth first, subtract as you go, and declare success when a leaf makes the remainder exactly zero.

sections.s2_technical:
The core idea is that a root-to-leaf path is naturally explored by recursion. We define a helper method `hasPath(node, target)` that returns a boolean. At each node we subtract the node's value from the target. If the node is a leaf, meaning both children are null, we return whether the remaining target now equals zero. For example, `if (node.left == null && node.right == null) return remaining == 0;` captures the leaf test precisely.

If the node is not a leaf, we recurse into whichever children exist and combine the results with a logical OR, because a single successful path anywhere is enough. For example, `return hasPath(node.left, remaining) || hasPath(node.right, remaining);` short-circuits as soon as one branch succeeds, which is a small but real efficiency win.

A senior-level nuance is the leaf definition. We must only declare success at a true leaf, not at a null child, otherwise a path that happens to pass through a node whose value equals the remaining target would falsely succeed even though the path has not ended. Another nuance is that values can be negative in general trees, so we cannot prune a branch early just because the remaining target went negative; we must reach a leaf to decide. In a banking fee model where every fee is positive we could prune, but the general algorithm does not assume that.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, a transfer request from Rajesh travels through a tree of approval desks. Each desk charges a processing fee in rupees, and the bank's compliance team wants to confirm that at least one complete approval chain, from the top desk down to a final signing desk, carries a total fee that matches an agreed budget exactly. This matters because a chain that overshoots or undershoots the budget indicates a misconfigured desk. This is exactly how Binary Tree Path Sum works: the running budget is the target, each desk's fee is a node value, and a final signing desk is a leaf.

Problem 2 — The compliance team does not care which chain matches, only whether any chain matches. This is why the algorithm returns a plain boolean and stops early on the first match, because once a valid chain is found the configuration is proven acceptable.

The code will define an `ApprovalNode` class holding a desk name and a `BigDecimal` fee plus left and right child desks. A `PathSumService` will expose `hasApprovalChainMatching(root, budget)` that drives a recursive depth-first search. A small `Demo` main method will build a sample approval tree for Rajesh's transfer and check two budgets, one that matches and one that does not, logging each descent.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the approval tree with Branch(100) as root, Regional(250) and Audit(150) as children, SignA(50) and SignB(400) under Regional, and a budget of 400.

Step 1: We enter at Branch with budget 400. We subtract the fee 100, leaving a remaining budget of 300. Branch is not a leaf, so we recurse left into Regional carrying 300.

Step 2: At Regional we subtract 250 from 300, leaving 50. Regional is not a leaf, so we recurse left into SignA carrying 50.

Step 3: At SignA we subtract 50 from 50, leaving exactly 0. SignA is a leaf, and the remaining budget equals zero, so this branch returns true.

Step 4: The true result short-circuits back up through Regional and Branch, so we never explore Audit or SignB. The final answer is true.

```

FINE: Visiting desk Regional fee=250 remainingBudget=50
FINE: Visiting desk SignA fee=50 remainingBudget=0
INFO: Chain ends at signing desk SignA — budget matched exactly

```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: budget=400, root=Branch(fee=100)
    │
    ▼
  Branch(100)  remaining = 400-100 = 300
    │ not leaf → recurse left
    ▼
  Regional(250)  remaining = 300-250 = 50
    ├─ left  → SignA(50)  remaining = 50-50 = 0  → LEAF, 0 → true
    └─ right → SignB(400) (never visited, OR short-circuits)
    │
    ▼
  Audit(150) subtree never visited (left branch already true)
    │
    ▼
  Result: true   (chain Branch→Regional→SignA sums to 400)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Binary Tree Path Sum asks whether any root-to-leaf path in a binary tree adds up to a given target, and it is a classic Tree Depth First Search problem. I solve it recursively: at each node I subtract the node's value from the running target, and when I reach a leaf I check whether the remaining target is exactly zero. For internal nodes I combine the results of the left and right recursions with a logical OR, so the search stops as soon as one valid path is found. The traversal visits each node once, giving linear time, and the recursion stack uses space proportional to the height of the tree.

The single most important correctness detail is the leaf test. I only declare success at a true leaf, where both children are null, never at a null child, because otherwise a path that merely passes through a node whose value equals the remaining target would falsely succeed before the path actually ends. I also keep in mind that node values can be negative in a general tree, so I cannot prune a branch just because the remaining target went below zero; I must descend to a leaf to decide.

In my work at the National Bank of India I used this exact pattern to validate approval-fee chains. A transfer request from Rajesh flowed through a tree of approval desks, each charging a processing fee, and compliance needed to confirm that at least one full top-to-bottom chain carried fees summing precisely to an agreed budget. I modelled each desk as a node with a BigDecimal fee, drove the depth-first search from the top desk, and returned true the moment a signing desk closed a chain at exactly zero remaining budget. Explaining the leaf-only success rule and the money-safe BigDecimal comparison is what shows an interviewer I understand both the algorithm and its real banking consequences.
